'''Joan Roughgarden''' (born March 13, 1946) is an American theoretical [[ecologist]] and [[evolutionary biologist]]. She is professor of biology and of geophysics emerita at [[Stanford University]] and an adjunct researcher at the [[Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology]]. She combined mathematical theory with field studies of Caribbean ''[[Anolis]]'' lizards and of larval recruitment in rocky-intertidal barnacles, wrote textbooks in ecological and evolutionary theory, and founded Stanford's Earth Systems Program.

From the 2000s she also became known outside ecology for books and papers criticizing Darwin's theory of [[sexual selection]] and proposing an alternative she called social selection. Secondary sources have treated her survey of sexual and gender diversity in animals as influential in public and interdisciplinary discussion, while describing the proposed replacement of sexual selection as contested.<ref name="Allen2014">{{cite journal |last=Allen |first=Arthur |title=Sexual Selection's Mystique Lingers |journal=BioScience |volume=64 |issue=5 |year=2014 |pages=375–380 |doi=10.1093/biosci/biu047}}</ref><ref name="Scientist2006">{{cite news |last=Atkinson |first=Nick |title=Sexual selection alternative slammed |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/sexual-selection-alternative-slammed-47558 |work=The Scientist |date=May 5, 2006 |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref> She is a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and received the 2005 [[Stonewall Book Award]] for ''Evolution's Rainbow''.

== Early life and education ==
Roughgarden was born in [[Paterson, New Jersey]]. She received a B.S. in biology, and a B.A. in philosophy from the [[University of Rochester]] in 1968, and an M.S. and Ph.D. in biology from [[Harvard University]] in 1971. Her doctoral work on density-dependent natural selection, supervised by [[William H. Bossert]], appeared the same year as a paper in ''[[Ecology (journal)|Ecology]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Roughgarden |first=J. |title=Density-Dependent Natural Selection |journal=Ecology |volume=52 |issue=3 |year=1971 |pages=453–468 |doi=10.2307/1937628 |jstor=1937628}}</ref>

In 1998 she came out as [[transgender]].<ref name="NYT2000">{{cite news |last=Yoon |first=Carol Kaesuk |title=Scientist at Work: Joan Roughgarden |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/10/17/science/scientist-work-joan-roughgarden-theorist-with-personal-experience-divide-between.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=October 17, 2000 |access-date=March 7, 2014}}</ref>

== Career ==
She taught at the [[University of Massachusetts Boston]] from 1970 to 1972, then joined Stanford's Department of Biology in 1972. She was also appointed in geophysics and remained at Stanford until retiring in 2011 as professor of biology and of geophysics emerita.<ref>{{cite web |title=Joan Roughgarden |url=https://profiles.stanford.edu/joan-roughgarden |publisher=Stanford University |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref> From 1992 to 1999 she founded and directed Stanford's Earth Systems Program.<ref>{{cite web |title=About |url=https://earthsystems.stanford.edu/about |publisher=Earth Systems Program, Stanford University |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref>

As of 2026 she lived in Santa Rosa, California.<ref name="PD2026">{{cite news |title=Documentary about sex, gender highlights groundbreaking work of Santa Rosa biologist |url=https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/07/25/new-documentary-highlights-groundbreaking-work-of-santa-rosa-biologist/ |newspaper=The Press Democrat |date=July 25, 2026 |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==

=== Ecological theory, anoles, and intertidal recruitment ===
The 1971 density-dependence paper and the 1979 textbook ''Theory of Population Genetics and Evolutionary Ecology'' presented a mathematical link between ecological population dynamics and gene-frequency change. The textbook was reprinted in 1987 and 1996.<ref>{{cite book |last=Roughgarden |first=J. |title=Theory of Population Genetics and Evolutionary Ecology: An Introduction |publisher=Macmillan |year=1979}}</ref>

In the 1970s and 1980s she and collaborators used eastern-Caribbean ''Anolis'' lizards as a model for competition and eco-evolutionary dynamics, work later collected in ''Anolis Lizards of the Caribbean'' (1995). Enclosure experiments with Stephen Pacala showed that the strength of interspecific competition increased with overlap in body size.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pacala |first1=Stephen W. |last2=Roughgarden |first2=J. |title=Population Experiments with the Anolis Lizards of St. Maarten and St. Eustatius |journal=Ecology |volume=66 |issue=1 |year=1985 |pages=129–141 |doi=10.2307/1941313}}</ref> Reviews of eco-evolutionary feedbacks have cited the anole system, developed further by [[Jonathan Losos]] and others, as a leading example of [[adaptive radiation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Post |first1=David M. |last2=Palkovacs |first2=Eric P. |title=Eco-evolutionary feedbacks in community and ecosystem ecology |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B |volume=364 |issue=1523 |year=2009 |pages=1629–1640 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2009.0012 |pmc=2690506 |pmid=19414476}}</ref>

At the [[Hopkins Marine Station]] she studied rocky-intertidal barnacles. With Steve Gaines and later Sean Connolly she argued that adult predation and competition structure communities mainly where oceanography allows dense settlement, whereas in central California barnacle numbers tracked pulsed larval recruitment after relaxation of upwelling.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gaines |first1=S. |last2=Roughgarden |first2=J. |title=Larval settlement rate: A leading determinant of structure in an ecological community of the marine intertidal zone |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=82 |issue=11 |year=1985 |pages=3707–3711 |doi=10.1073/pnas.82.11.3707 |pmc=397856 |pmid=16593571}}</ref> They related a latitudinal gradient in west-coast upwelling to stronger adult interactions in the north and stronger recruitment limitation in the south.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Connolly |first1=Sean R. |last2=Roughgarden |first2=J. |title=A Latitudinal Gradient in Northeast Pacific Intertidal Community Structure |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=151 |issue=4 |year=1998 |pages=311–326 |doi=10.1086/286121 |pmid=18811323}}</ref>

With colleagues she also published on fishery collapse and the economics of ecological stability. Roughgarden and Smith argued that ecologically stable fishery management places the target stock on the right-hand side of the production curve, above the stock producing maximum sustainable yield, making the stock less vulnerable to collapse.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=J. |last2=Smith |first2=F. |title=Why fisheries collapse and what to do about it |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=93 |issue=10 |year=1996 |pages=5078–5083 |doi=10.1073/pnas.93.10.5078 |pmc=39409 |pmid=11607680}}</ref> In related work with Paul Armsworth, she examined the economic value of ecological stability.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Armsworth |first1=Paul R. |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Joan E. |title=The economic value of ecological stability |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=100 |issue=12 |year=2003 |pages=7147–7151 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0832226100 |pmc=165844 |pmid=12777632}}</ref>

=== Sexual selection and social selection ===
In ''Evolution's Rainbow: Diversity, Gender, and Sexuality in Nature and People'' (2004; tenth-anniversary edition 2013), Roughgarden argued that standard sexual-selection theory does not account for the range of animal mating systems, sex change, multiple morphs within a sex, and same-sex sexual behavior.<ref name="Rainbow">{{cite book |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=Evolution's Rainbow |publisher=University of California Press |year=2013 |edition=Tenth anniversary}}</ref> She proposed “social selection,” defined as selection on differential offspring production through social interaction rather than on differential mating success alone.<ref>{{cite book |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=The Genial Gene: Deconstructing Darwinian Selfishness |publisher=University of California Press |year=2009}}</ref> On her account, sexual selection focuses on mating success and on competition, conflict, and genetic quality, whereas social selection focuses on offspring delivery and on negotiation, teamwork, and division of labor.<ref name="BSD2025">{{cite journal |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=Explaining sex: contrast between social and sexual selection |journal=Biology of Sex Differences |volume=17 |issue=1 |year=2025 |article-number=12 |doi=10.1186/s13293-025-00807-3 |doi-access=free |pmid=41476243 |pmc=12837013}}</ref>

The book received the 2005 Stonewall Book Award for nonfiction and has been translated into Portuguese, Korean, and Spanish.<ref>{{cite web |title=ALA announces 2005 Stonewall Book award winner |url=https://www.ala.org/news/news/pressreleases2005/january2005/2005stonewallwinner |publisher=American Library Association |access-date=October 17, 2024}}</ref> Reviews treated the natural-history survey as valuable while dividing over the theoretical claim that social selection should replace sexual selection.<ref>{{cite news |last=Rose |first=Steven |title=Chat-up lines |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2004/aug/21/featuresreviews.guardianreview4 |newspaper=The Guardian |date=August 21, 2004 |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Dorit |first=Robert |title=Rethinking Sex |magazine=American Scientist |volume=92 |issue=5 |date=September–October 2004 |doi=10.1511/2004.49.0 |url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/rethinking-sex |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref> [[Douglas J. Futuyma]] reviewed it in ''[[Evolution (journal)|Evolution]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Futuyma |first=Douglas J. |title=Celebrating Diversity in Sexuality and Gender |journal=Evolution |volume=59 |issue=5 |year=2005 |pages=1156–1159 |doi=10.1554/BR05-4}}</ref> The book has been cited beyond evolutionary biology, including in discussions of sex and gender in the humanities and social sciences, and it continues to appear in popular-science treatments of animal sexual diversity, among them Nathan H. Lents's 2025 book ''The Sexual Evolution''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sinclair |first=Rebekah |title=Joan Roughgarden. Evolution's Rainbow: Diversity, Gender, and Sexuality in Nature and People |journal=Women's Studies |volume=43 |issue=5 |year=2014 |pages=678–684 |doi=10.1080/00497878.2014.914411}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Graff |first=Gordon |title=On the Originality of Species |magazine=Stanford Magazine |date=May–June 2004 |url=https://stanfordmag.org/contents/on-the-originality-of-species |access-date=September 13, 2026}}</ref> A 2025–2026 documentary, ''Second Nature: Gender and Sexuality in the Animal World'', directed by Drew Denny and narrated by [[Elliot Page]], featured her work on that subject.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=White |first=Abbey |title='Second Nature' Director on the Science Behind Queerness in the Animal Kingdom |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/second-nature-director-elliot-page-lgbtqia-representation-animals-1236423229/ |magazine=The Hollywood Reporter |date=November 10, 2025 |access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref>

A 2006 article in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', with Erol Akçay and Meeko Oishi, recast some aspects of reproductive behavior in cooperative-game terms and argued that sexual selection should be replaced.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=Joan |last2=Oishi |first2=Meeko |last3=Akçay |first3=Erol |title=Reproductive Social Behavior: Cooperative Games to Replace Sexual Selection |journal=Science |volume=311 |issue=5763 |year=2006 |pages=965–969 |doi=10.1126/science.1110105 |pmid=16484485}}</ref> Forty biologists published ten critical letters. Correspondents said the paper misrepresented sexual-selection theory and that the alternative did not explain data accounted for by the existing theory. Roughgarden replied that the dissent was expected and that social selection was not an extension of sexual selection.<ref name="Scientist2006" /><ref>{{cite journal |title=Debating Sexual Selection and Mating Strategies |journal=Science |volume=312 |issue=5774 |year=2006 |pages=689–697 |doi=10.1126/science.312.5774.689b |pmid=16675684}}</ref> [[Tim Clutton-Brock]], in a 2007 ''Science'' review, accepted that sexual selection can act on females as well as males but treated the framework as robust.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Clutton-Brock |first=Tim |title=Sexual Selection in Males and Females |journal=Science |volume=318 |issue=5858 |year=2007 |pages=1882–1885 |doi=10.1126/science.1133311 |pmid=18096798}}</ref> In 2010 Roughgarden and Akçay replied in ''[[Animal Behaviour (journal)|Animal Behaviour]]'' that extending sexual selection to females did not resolve what they regarded as contradictions in the framework, and they argued against redefining sexual selection as a “version 2.0” rather than replacing it.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=J. |last2=Akçay |first2=E. |title=Do we need a Sexual Selection 2.0? |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=79 |issue=3 |year=2010 |pages=e1–e4 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2009.06.006}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=J. |last2=Akçay |first2=E. |title=Final response: sexual selection needs an alternative |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=79 |issue=3 |year=2010 |pages=e18–e23 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2009.12.029}}</ref>

In a 2014 ''BioScience'' feature, Arthur Allen described the proposed replacement as remaining outside the mainstream of evolutionary biology.<ref name="Allen2014" /> In a 2019 interview Roughgarden said that most biologists remained defensive of sexual selection.<ref>{{cite web |title=Q&A with Joan Roughgarden on the Problems with the Theory of Sexual Selection |url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/blog/qa-joan-roughgarden-problems-theory-sexual-selection |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613223917/https://mitpress.mit.edu/blog/qa-joan-roughgarden-problems-theory-sexual-selection |archive-date=June 13, 2021 |url-status=dead |publisher=MIT Press |date=February 11, 2019 |access-date=September 13, 2026}}</ref>

In 2025 she published a further comparison of the two frameworks in ''[[Biology of Sex Differences]]'', setting out 26 points of disagreement. The paper contrasts the frameworks on questions including why sexual reproduction exists; why males, females, and hermaphrodites exist; what sex roles occur; whether males form a hierarchy of genetic quality; how many genders exist; and what function affiliative behavior, including same-sex mating, serves.<ref name="BSD2025" />

=== Theistic evolution ===
In ''Evolution and Christian Faith'' (2006) Roughgarden argued that evolutionary biology need not conflict with Christian scripture and opposed both [[creationism]] and [[intelligent design]] while affirming [[theistic evolution]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=Evolution and Christian Faith |publisher=Island Press |year=2006}}</ref>

=== Holobionts ===
After retirement she published models of the holobiont (a host plus its microbial symbionts) and of related hologenome ideas associated with [[Lynn Margulis]] and with Ilana Zilber-Rosenberg and Eugene Rosenberg. A 2018 review with Scott F. Gilbert and others treated holobionts as possible units of selection.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=Joan |last2=Gilbert |first2=Scott F. |last3=Rosenberg |first3=Eugene |last4=Zilber-Rosenberg |first4=Ilana |last5=Lloyd |first5=Elisabeth A. |title=Holobionts as Units of Selection and a Model of Their Population Dynamics and Evolution |journal=Biological Theory |volume=13 |year=2018 |pages=44–65 |doi=10.1007/s13752-017-0287-1}}</ref> Subsequent papers distinguished vertical from horizontal microbial transmission.<ref name="AN2023">{{cite journal |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=Holobiont Evolution: Population Theory for the Hologenome |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=201 |issue=6 |year=2023 |pages=763–778 |doi=10.1086/723782 |pmid=37229712|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Whether hosts and their microbes evolve as a unit is disputed. Nancy A. Moran and Daniel B. Sloan argued that limited vertical transmission undercuts hologenome selection; a 2019 news feature in the ''Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences'' described the debate as unresolved.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moran |first1=Nancy A. |last2=Sloan |first2=Daniel B. |title=The Hologenome Concept: Helpful or Hollow? |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=13 |issue=12 |year=2015 |article-number=e1002311 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1002311 |doi-access=free |pmc=4670207 |pmid=26636661}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Beans |first=Carolyn |title=Do hosts and their microbes evolve as a unit? |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=116 |issue=29 |year=2019 |pages=14377–14380 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1908139116 |pmc=6642426 |pmid=31308236}}</ref> In 2023 Roughgarden's model showed that holobiont selection was possible with horizontal microbial transmission, but she argued that host-controlled assembly of the microbiome was more important in explaining microbiome–host integration.<ref name="AN2023" /> Related phage–bacteria models appeared in 2024 and 2026.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=Lytic/Lysogenic Transition as a Life-History Switch |journal=Virus Evolution |volume=10 |issue=1 |year=2024 |article-number=veae028 |doi=10.1093/ve/veae028 |doi-access=free |pmid=38756985 |pmc=11097211}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Roughgarden |first=Joan |title=Evolutionarily Optimal Phage Life-History Traits: Burst Size vs. Lysis Time |journal=Viruses |volume=18 |issue=8 |year=2026 |article-number=814 |doi=10.3390/v18080814 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=October 2026}}
* Stonewall Book Award (nonfiction), 2005
* Center Fellow, [[National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis]], 1998
* Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel Award, Stanford University, 1995
* Visiting research fellow, [[Merton College, Oxford]], 1994
* Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, 1993
* [[Guggenheim Fellowship]], 1985
* University Fellow, Stanford University, 1978

She has served as associate editor of ''The American Naturalist'' (1984–1989), ''Oecologia'' (1979–1982), ''Theoretical Population Biology'' (1975–1986), and ''Philosophy and Theory in Biology'' (from 2008), and as chair of the Theoretical Ecology Section of the [[Ecological Society of America]] (2002–2003).

* Roughgarden, Joan. ''Anolis Lizards of the Caribbean: Ecology, Evolution and Plate Tectonics''. Oxford University Press, 1995.
* Roughgarden, Joan. ''Primer of Ecological Theory''. Prentice Hall, 1997.
* Roughgarden, Joan. ''Evolution's Rainbow: Diversity, Gender and Sexuality in Nature and People''. University of California Press, 2004.
* Roughgarden, Joan. ''Evolution and Christian Faith''. Island Press, 2006.
* Roughgarden, Joan. ''The Genial Gene: Deconstructing Darwinian Selfishness''. University of California Press, 2009.
* Roughgarden, Joan. ''Ram-2050: A Ramayana Epic for the Future''. Kauai Institute, 2015.
